subtitle: Recognize harassment and disrespectful conduct, respond as a bystander, build psychologically safe team habits and route concerns to the right office.
audience: For all DHS and DSD employees, including supervisors, who want shared language and practical options for a respectful workplace. It does not replace HR, EOAD or legal advice.

lessons.title: What harassment and a respectful workplace mean
objectives: Distinguish the legal definition of harassment from the broader conduct standard in state respectful workplace policy.
Identify the protected classes named in federal law and in the Minnesota Human Rights Act.
Explain why an employee does not have to decide which policy applies before raising a concern.
Recognize examples of disrespectful conduct named in state policy, including deliberate misgendering and deliberate mispronunciation of names.
lessons.teaching:
People use the word harassment loosely, so it helps to separate three layers. The first is the law. The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission describes harassment as unwelcome conduct based on a protected characteristic such as race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age forty and older, disability or genetic information. Under federal law it becomes illegal when putting up with it becomes a condition of keeping the job, or when it is severe or pervasive enough that a reasonable person would find the workplace intimidating, hostile or abusive. The EEOC is clear that petty slights and isolated incidents, unless extremely serious, usually do not reach that legal line.

The second layer is Minnesota law. The Minnesota Human Rights Act protects more groups than federal law does. The Minnesota Department of Human Rights lists race, religion, disability, national origin, sex, marital status, familial status, age, sexual orientation and gender identity among the protected classes, and the Act also prohibits reprisal against people who assert their rights. Age protection under state law starts at the age of majority rather than at forty.

The third layer is state and agency policy, and this is where most everyday conduct is addressed. Minnesota Management and Budget sets statewide human resources policies for executive branch agencies. Its Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited policy covers unwelcome conduct tied to protected class, including offensive jokes, slurs, and deliberate misgendering or mispronunciation of a name. Its Respectful Workplace policy covers disrespectful conduct that is not tied to protected class: shouting, threats, demeaning or humiliating treatment, bullying, and sabotaging someone's work. DHS has its own policies that follow the same pattern. Policy standards are deliberately set below the legal line, so an employer can correct behavior before it becomes a legal problem.

Here is the practical point. You do not have to decide whether something is illegal harassment, a policy violation or just a bad day before you raise it. Sorting that out is the job of Human Resources and the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division. Your job is to notice, to respond in a way that is safe, and to route the concern to people who can act. This course builds shared language for doing that. It does not make anyone an investigator or a legal decision-maker.
lessons.keyPoint: Law sets the floor, policy sets a higher standard for daily conduct, and you do not need to classify a concern before raising it. Classification belongs to HR and EOAD.
lessons.example: Fictional case: In a DSD policy team meeting, Corwin keeps calling a coworker, Ilse, by a shortened nickname she has asked him not to use. He jokes that her full name is too hard. Later, in a message thread, he mocks her accent. Ilse's teammate Marguerite notices both. Marguerite is not sure whether this counts as harassment or just rudeness, and she worries that if she calls it harassment and is wrong, she will look like she is overreacting.
lessons.question: What is the most useful way for Marguerite to think about what she saw?
choices: Wait until she is certain the conduct meets the legal definition of harassment before saying anything.
Recognize that the conduct may fall under state policy whether or not it is illegal, and that she can raise it without deciding which category it fits.
Decide it is only rudeness, since one nickname and one joke are isolated incidents.
feedback: The legal line is not the threshold for raising a concern. Policy reaches conduct well below it, and waiting for certainty usually means waiting too long.

This is the best response. Deliberately mispronouncing a name and mocking an accent are examples the state policies name. Marguerite can describe what she saw and let HR or EOAD determine how it is classified.

Repeated conduct after a request to stop is not an isolated incident, and conduct linked to national origin may fall under the harassment policy. Deciding it is minor on Ilse's behalf is not Marguerite's call.
lessons.reflection: Think about a time you hesitated to name something at work because you were not sure it was serious enough. What would have helped you feel able to raise it without first having to judge it?
lessons.action: Find the current DHS respectful workplace and harassment and discrimination policies on the DHS intranet or through your HR contact. Note in your own words one example of conduct each policy names, and where each policy says to report.

check.question: Why do state respectful workplace and harassment policies reach conduct that may not be illegal?
check.correct: So the employer can address and correct harmful conduct early, before it becomes severe or pervasive.
wrong: Because state policy replaces federal law for state employees.
Because every rude comment is illegal under the Minnesota Human Rights Act.
check.feedback: Policy is intentionally set above the legal floor. It lets supervisors, HR and EOAD address conduct early. It does not replace federal law, and not every rude act is illegal. The value of the policy is that you can raise a concern without proving a legal case.

lessons.title: Bystander action: the five Ds at work
objectives: Describe the five bystander strategies: distract, delegate, document, delay and direct.
Choose a bystander response that fits the safety, setting and wishes of the person targeted.
Explain why documentation belongs to the person who was targeted and must not be shared without their consent.
Identify how a supervisor's duty to report changes what bystander action looks like for them.
lessons.teaching:
Most harmful conduct at work happens in front of other people. Research and practice on bystander action start from a simple observation: people often want to help but freeze because they do not know what to do or fear making things worse. Right To Be, a national nonprofit that trains people to respond to harassment, teaches five options, known as the five Ds. Having more than one option matters, because the right response depends on safety, setting and what the targeted person wants.

Distract means interrupting the moment without confronting anyone. In a meeting, that might be changing the subject, asking the targeted person a work question, or calling a short break. Delegate means bringing in someone with more authority or a better position to act, such as a supervisor, a meeting chair or HR. Document means making a factual note of what happened: date, time, words used and who was present. Right To Be stresses that you should always ask the targeted person what they want done with any record, and never share it without their permission. In a state agency, remember that notes you create on state systems may be government data, so keep them factual and share them only through proper channels. Delay means checking in afterward: saying that what happened was not okay, asking what the person needs and offering to go with them to report. Direct means naming the behavior briefly, such as saying that comment was not okay, but only when it is safe and when direct action is likely to help rather than escalate.

Two limits are important. First, bystander action is not investigation. You are not gathering evidence, interviewing coworkers or deciding what happened. Second, supervisors carry an added duty. Statewide policy requires managers and supervisors to report protected-class harassment or discrimination they learn about to HR or the agency affirmative action officer, and DHS policy directs supervisors to refer complaints to the Equal Opportunity and Access Division. A supervisor can still distract or check in, but cannot agree to keep protected-class harassment secret.

Delay is often the most underused option. A quiet follow-up can reduce isolation, and the person who was targeted keeps control over what happens next.
lessons.keyPoint: There is always something you can do. Choose the option that is safe, fits the setting and respects what the targeted person wants, and route concerns rather than investigating them.
lessons.example: Fictional case: During a video call with county partners, a DHS contractor named Garrick makes a joke about a program participant's religion. The DSD staff member who organized the call, Tamsin, sees her colleague Yusra go quiet with her camera off. Tamsin is not a supervisor. The call has twenty minutes left, and several partners are senior to her. Afterward, Tamsin wonders whether she missed her chance to do anything.
lessons.question: What is the most helpful thing Tamsin can do now that the call is over?
choices: Check in privately with Yusra, say that the comment was not okay, ask what she needs, and offer information about reporting routes, including telling the contract manager.
Email Garrick and the county partners describing the comment so everyone knows it was unacceptable.
Record everything she remembers and forward it to HR right away without talking to Yusra.
feedback: This is the best response. It uses delay, respects Yusra's control over next steps and opens a path to report. Because the speaker is a contractor, the contract manager and HR are appropriate routes for addressing his conduct.
Public calling out in a group email can escalate, expose Yusra without her consent and bypass the people responsible for addressing contractor conduct.
Making a factual note is reasonable, but sending it before speaking with Yusra removes her choice. Unless Tamsin is a supervisor with a duty to report, she should ask Yusra first.
lessons.reflection: Which of the five Ds feels most natural to you, and which feels hardest? What would make the hardest one easier to use in your actual meetings?
lessons.action: Write down two short phrases you could use in a meeting to distract or direct, and one sentence you could use to check in with a coworker afterward. Keep them somewhere you will see them before your next large meeting.

check.question: According to Right To Be, what should a bystander do with a recording or note of a harassment incident?
check.correct: Ask the person who was targeted what they want done with it, and not share it without their permission.
wrong: Post it so others can see the behavior was witnessed.
Keep it private and never mention it to anyone, including the person targeted.
check.feedback: Documentation exists to support the person who was targeted. Sharing without consent can harm them and take away their choices. Keeping it secret from them also removes their choice. Supervisors have separate reporting duties under state policy.

lessons.title: Psychological safety as team practices
objectives: Explain Amy Edmondson's definition of team psychological safety.
Distinguish psychological safety from comfort, niceness or lowered standards.
Identify at least four observable practices that build or erode psychological safety on a team.
Plan how a leader takes responsibility for repair after a comment or decision lands badly.
lessons.teaching:
Amy Edmondson, a researcher at Harvard Business School, defined team psychological safety as a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking. Interpersonal risks are ordinary work acts that could make someone look ignorant, incompetent or disruptive: asking a question, admitting a mistake, raising a concern or disagreeing with a more senior person. In her study of work teams in a manufacturing company, psychological safety was associated with more learning behavior, and learning behavior was associated with better team performance. That study, like much of the later research, shows association rather than proof that one causes the other, but the pattern has been repeated in many settings.

Psychological safety is not the same as being nice, avoiding conflict or lowering expectations. A team can hold high standards and still make it safe to say that something is not working. In fact, candor is what lets high standards be met. It is also a team-level condition. It describes how a group works, not a personality trait that some staff have and others lack.

Because it is a condition, it is built through practices that anyone can observe. Make disagreement normal: before deciding, ask for the strongest case against your own idea, and thank the person who raised a concern in front of others. Separate unfamiliarity from intentional harm: most awkward moments at work come from not knowing, and the right response is information and a chance to change. Intentional harm goes to the formal channels. Put repair on the person with more power: when a comment or decision lands badly, the leader names it and takes responsibility, and the person harmed is not asked to explain, educate or forgive on a schedule. Show that input changed something: regularly say what changed because someone spoke up, and if nothing did, say why. Watch the grind: constant urgency silences people, so protect time for thinking and for saying no.

None of this replaces the confidential and formal channels. A team with good habits still routes complaints of harassment and discrimination to HR and EOAD. Psychological safety makes it more likely people will speak up early. It does not make the supervisor an investigator.
lessons.keyPoint: Psychological safety is a shared belief that interpersonal risk is safe here. It is built by observable habits, especially how leaders respond to disagreement, mistakes and harm.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Rosalind supervises a DSD waiver policy team. In a planning meeting, she dismisses a concern from a newer analyst, Obi, about a notice that he thinks will confuse families, saying there is no time to revisit it. Two weeks later a county partner raises the same problem. Rosalind notices that Obi has stopped speaking in meetings. She wants to fix the damage without making Obi feel singled out.
lessons.question: What should Rosalind do next?
choices: Tell Obi privately that he should speak up more, since his concerns are clearly valuable.
Wait for Obi to raise it himself, so he feels in control.
At the next team meeting, name that Obi raised this concern first, say she should have listened, explain what will change in the notice and how she will handle concerns in future.
feedback: Encouragement is kind, but it puts the burden back on Obi and does not repair what happened in front of the team.
Waiting puts repair on the person with less power. The leader, who made the misstep, should act first.
This is the best response. Rosalind takes responsibility in the same setting where the harm happened, credits Obi, shows that input changes decisions and commits to a practice change.
lessons.reflection: Think of a team where you felt free to disagree. What did the leader or group do that made that possible? Which of those habits do you practice yourself?
lessons.action: In your next meeting, try one practice: ask for the strongest case against a proposal, or close by saying one thing that changed because someone raised it. Notice what happens.

check.question: Which statement best describes psychological safety as Edmondson defined it?
check.correct: A shared belief among team members that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking.
wrong: A policy that guarantees no one will ever feel uncomfortable at work.
A personality trait of confident employees who speak up easily.
check.feedback: Edmondson's definition is about a team-level belief shaped by how the group behaves. It does not promise comfort, and it is not a trait of individuals. Discomfort is normal when learning. The question is whether speaking up is punished.

lessons.title: Reporting routes: route, do not investigate
objectives: Identify the internal and external routes for raising respectful workplace, harassment and discrimination concerns.
Explain why supervisors refer protected-class complaints promptly and do not investigate them.
Describe what retaliation is and why it is prohibited.
Draft a brief, factual referral that shares only what is needed.
lessons.teaching:
Knowing where to go is part of a respectful workplace. State and DHS policies give several routes, and a person can choose the one that feels safest. For respectful workplace concerns, statewide policy lists the employee's supervisor, the agency Human Resources office, a union representative and the Employee Assistance Program as places to start, and it encourages informal resolution where that is safe and appropriate. For harassment or discrimination tied to a protected class, statewide policy lists supervisors and managers, the agency affirmative action officer and the HR office. At DHS, the Equal Opportunity and Access Division handles discrimination, harassment and retaliation complaints. People can also go outside the agency to the Minnesota Department of Human Rights or the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which have their own filing deadlines.

Supervisors have a specific duty. Statewide policy requires managers and supervisors to report allegations of protected-class harassment or discrimination to HR or the affirmative action officer right away, and DHS policy directs supervisors to refer complaints to EOAD. DHS policy is also clear that supervisors do not investigate these complaints themselves. That means a supervisor should not interview witnesses, ask the person to prove what happened, confront the person accused, or try to mediate a protected-class complaint. Well-meant investigating can compromise a fair process, expose private data and put the person who raised the concern at risk. A supervisor's job is to listen, make sure the person is safe, refer promptly and keep the matter to people who need to know.

Retaliation is prohibited. Under state policy and the Minnesota Human Rights Act, no one may be punished for reporting, opposing harassment or discrimination, or taking part in an investigation. Retaliation can be obvious, like a worse assignment, or subtle, like being left out of meetings. Watch for it, and route it the same way.

Finally, be careful with information. Complaint information is sensitive. Share what is needed with the office that will act, keep your own notes factual, and do not discuss the matter with coworkers. If you are unsure which route fits, contact HR or EOAD and ask. Asking is never the wrong step.
lessons.keyPoint: Everyone can raise a concern through several routes. Supervisors listen, keep people safe and refer promptly to HR or EOAD. They never investigate protected-class complaints themselves.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Anneliese, a DSD unit supervisor, is approached by Desmond, a case management consultant, who says a colleague has made repeated comments about his disability and has joked about his accommodation in front of others. Desmond asks Anneliese to keep it between them and just talk to the colleague informally. Anneliese wants to respect Desmond's wishes and fix the problem quickly.
lessons.question: What should Anneliese do?
choices: Thank Desmond, explain that as a supervisor she must refer disability-related harassment concerns to EOAD or HR, tell him what to expect, check whether he needs anything to feel safe at work and make the referral promptly.
Agree to keep it confidential and speak to the colleague informally to stop the jokes.
Interview the coworkers who were present to confirm Desmond's account before deciding whether to refer it.
feedback: This is the best response. Anneliese is honest about her duty, keeps Desmond informed and safe, and routes the concern to the office responsible for determining what happened.
A supervisor cannot promise to keep protected-class harassment confidential. Handling it informally skips the required referral and may leave Desmond without protection.
Supervisors do not investigate protected-class complaints. Interviewing witnesses can compromise the formal process and spread private information.
lessons.reflection: If someone brought you a concern tomorrow, would you know which route fits? What would you need to look up or ask so you feel prepared?
lessons.action: Find and save the current contact route for DHS EOAD, your HR business partner and the Employee Assistance Program. If you supervise, review with HR what your referral duty looks like in practice.

check.question: Why do supervisors refer protected-class harassment complaints instead of investigating them?
check.correct: Because the responsible office conducts a fair process, and supervisor investigating can compromise it, expose private information and put the reporting employee at risk.
wrong: Because supervisors are not allowed to listen to complaints at all.
Because referral is only needed when the supervisor believes the complaint is true.
check.feedback: Supervisors should listen carefully and support the employee. What they do not do is determine what happened. Referral does not depend on whether the supervisor believes the account. The office responsible for investigation makes that determination.

cards.back: Unwelcome conduct based on a protected characteristic that becomes a condition of employment or is severe or pervasive enough to create a hostile work environment.
Statewide and DHS policy covering disrespectful conduct such as shouting, bullying and demeaning treatment, including conduct that is not tied to a protected class.
Distract, delegate, document, delay and direct: five bystander options taught by Right To Be. Choose the one that is safe and fits what the targeted person wants.
Edmondson's term for a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, such as asking questions, admitting mistakes or disagreeing.
Negative treatment of someone because they reported, opposed or took part in an investigation of harassment or discrimination. It is prohibited.
The DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division, which receives and investigates discrimination, harassment and retaliation complaints.

aid.heading: When you witness something
items: Check safety first, for the targeted person and for you.
Pick one of the five Ds: distract, delegate, document, delay or direct.
Check in afterward and ask what the person needs.
Never share notes or recordings without the targeted person's consent unless you are a supervisor with a duty to report.
Do not investigate. Route the concern.

aid.heading: If someone brings you a concern
items: Listen, thank them and avoid judging whether it is serious enough.
Explain honestly what you can and cannot keep confidential.
Share the routes: supervisor, HR, EOAD, union representative, Employee Assistance Program, and external agencies.
If you are a supervisor and it involves a protected class, refer to HR or EOAD promptly.
Watch for and route any retaliation.

aid.heading: Team habits that build safety
items: Ask for the strongest case against your own idea before deciding.
Thank people who raise concerns, in front of others.
Respond to unfamiliarity with information and a chance to change.
When something lands badly, the person with more power leads the repair.
Say what changed because someone spoke up.

sources.title: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — Harassment
sources.note: Supports the federal definition of harassment, the protected characteristics, the condition-of-employment and severe-or-pervasive standards, and the note that petty slights are usually not illegal. Federal enforcement positions change, so check current EEOC guidance for any formal question.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Rights — Minnesota Human Rights Act
sources.note: Supports the list of protected classes in employment under Minnesota law, including sexual orientation and gender identity, and the reprisal protection. Formal determinations rest with MDHR and the courts.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1432, Respectful Workplace (revised 2023)
sources.note: Supports the statewide definition of respectful conduct, examples of disrespectful behavior, the separation from protected-class harassment, and reporting routes including supervisor, HR, union representative and EAP.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1436, Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited (revised 2024)
sources.note: Supports examples of protected-class harassment including deliberate misgendering and name mispronunciation, supervisor duty to report immediately, and the retaliation prohibition.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Discrimination, Harassment and Retaliation Policy
sources.note: Supports that supervisors refer complaints to the Equal Opportunity and Access office and do not investigate. This public copy is an older version that uses a prior office name; learners should confirm current procedures on the DHS intranet.

sources.title: Right To Be — The 5Ds of Bystander Intervention
sources.note: Supports the five bystander strategies and the guidance to ask the targeted person before using any documentation. The workplace adaptations in this course are the program's own.

sources.title: Edmondson, A. — Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams, Administrative Science Quarterly (1999)
sources.note: Supports the definition of team psychological safety and its association with learning behavior in a field study of work teams. Findings are associational. The practice list in lesson three comes from program-owned material.
